procedural_history.originating_court: Judge, Family Courts, North Rohini, Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 28th January, 2015 in Petition No.363 of 2014, passed by the Judge, Family Courts, North Rohini, Delhi, to the limited extent of not granting maintenance amount to the appellant/wife from 10th December, 2010 onwards.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a revision petition before the High Court being Revision Petition (Criminal) No.204 of 2015, which has been partly allowed. The High Court partly allowed the revision petition preferred by the appellant and was pleased to set aside the judgment and order dated 28th January, 2015 in Petition No.363 of 2014, passed by the Judge, Family Courts, North Rohini, Delhi, to the limited extent of not granting maintenance amount to the appellant/wife from 10th December, 2010 onwards. The High Court instead directed the respondent/husband to pay the maintenance amount at the rate of Rs.9,000/- per month from 9th December, 2010 onwards to the appellant/ wife.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant has appealed the judgment and order passed by the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi dated May 31, 2018 in Revision Petition (Criminal) No.204 of 2015. The respondent has supported the decision of the High Court but argues that the impugned judgment suffers from flawed reasoning.

issue.issue_text: Whether the quantum of monthly maintenance amount determined by the High Court is just and proper.

facts: The Family Court had awarded the wife maintenance, but only for a limited period (July 2003 to December 2010).
The High Court extended the period of maintenance from December 2010 onwards but reduced the quantum to Rs. 9,000 per month.
During the proceedings, the Supreme Court had previously granted an interim maintenance of Rs. 20,000 per month.
The husband, who is highly qualified and able-bodied, claimed to be unemployed since 2010, despite earning over Rs. 1,77,364 per month in Canada in 2010.
law: When determining the quantum of maintenance, courts must have regard for the living standard of the parties, the earning capacity of the husband, and other relevant factors, not just a notional minimum income.
application: The Supreme Court found the High Court's reasoning for setting the maintenance at Rs. 9,000 per month to be "untenable."
The High Court had incorrectly based its calculation on the husband's notional minimum income according to Delhi's minimum wage laws.

The Supreme Court held that the High Court should have considered the husband's high living standard, his past conduct in delaying the case, and his significant past income (over Rs. 1.77 lakh/month).
The Court dismissed the husband's plea of unemployment as "specious and unsubstantiated," given that he is highly qualified and able-bodied.
The Court also noted that its own prior order granting Rs. 20,000 in interim maintenance should not have been reduced without a change in circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's determination as unjust and improper. To do complete justice and account for inflation and the cost of living, it modified the order, directing the husband to pay an enhanced maintenance of Rs. 20,000 per month from January 2010 and Rs. 25,000 per month from June 2018 onwards.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the quantum of monthly maintenance amount determined by the High Court is just and proper.
appellant_arguments: The appellant filed the appeal, taking exception to the judgment and order passed by the High Court, thereby arguing that the quantum of maintenance was not just and proper.
respondent_arguments: The respondent supported the decision of the High Court regarding the maintenance amount.
In a counter-affidavit, the respondent also argued that the High Court's judgment suffered from flawed reasoning, specifically that it did not deal with the reasoning of appreciation of evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An able-bodied man is presumed to be capable of earning sufficient money to reasonably maintain his wife and child, and he cannot claim an inability to earn to escape this legal obligation. The burden is on such a person to demonstrate to the court, with cogent grounds, that he is unable to earn enough for reasons beyond his control.
obiter: The laws of maintenance are intended to provide support, not to enrich, and maintenance payments cannot continue indefinitely.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's core finding is that an able-bodied, highly qualified man has a moral and legal duty to maintain his wife and is presumed to be capable of earning sufficiently to do so. His mere plea of having no source of income is not a valid defense to absolve him of this responsibility.
legal_tests_applied: "an able bodied young man has to be presumed to be capable of earning sufficient money so as to be able reasonably to maintain his wife and child and he cannot be heard to say that he is not in position to earn enough to be able to maintain them according to the family standard."

"The respondent’s mere plea that he does not possess any source of income ipso facto does not absolve himself of his moral duty to maintain his wife in presence of good physique along with educational qualification.”
why_appellant_lost: The final decision indicates the appeal was allowed, meaning the appellant was successful on the primary issue. Therefore, this section is not applicable.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was partially accepted to the extent that the Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's finding on the legal obligation to pay maintenance, stating that the finding recorded by the High Court on this point was "unassailable" and "un-exceptionable".
policy_considerations: The laws of maintenance are intended to provide support, not to enrich, and payments cannot continue ad-infinitum.
An able-bodied man has a moral duty to maintain his wife, and he cannot be heard to say that he is not in a position to earn enough to discharge his legal obligation.
